title: The Delegation Line
subtitle: Not what it can do — what you should let it do
summary: Twelve things that land on a desk in a normal week. For each one, decide how much of it you are willing to hand over.
takeaway: The question was never whether the tool is capable. It is whether a mistake would be visible to you before it reached somebody else. Where errors are obvious, delegate freely. Where errors are silent, do it yourself.

steps.title: Four positions on one line
steps.body:
This is not a question about capability. A model will attempt all twelve of these and produce something plausible every time. The question is what happens to a mistake.

**Do it myself** — the work is the judgement, and there is nothing to hand over.

**Draft and review** — it produces a first version, you read every word before it goes anywhere.

**It does it, I spot-check** — you look at a sample rather than the whole thing, because an error would be obvious if it were there.

**Never** — the material is protected, or a mistake would be silent and expensive.

steps.title: Twelve things from an ordinary week
steps.body: Some of these are close calls, and a couple are close calls in a direction people usually get wrong.
steps.prompt: Decide how far across the line each one goes.

items.text: Write the reminder email that goes out before every registration deadline.
items.why: Repetitive, low stakes, and you were going to proofread it anyway. This is the pattern that pays for itself — the same message, forty times a year.

items.text: Tell a student their financial aid appeal was denied.
items.why: The work here is not the words. Somebody is about to have a bad afternoon, and how it is delivered is the entire job. Use a template if you like, but write this one.

items.text: Turn twelve pages of committee notes into draft minutes.
items.why: A transform, with the original sitting right next to it. You can see what changed, which is exactly the condition that makes delegation safe.

items.text: Summarise a ninety-page board packet so your director can skip reading it.
items.why: Not because summarising is forbidden — because of what this one is *for*. A summary that decides where you read is useful. A summary that replaces reading puts a silent omission into somebody else's decision.

items.text: Reformat a messy roster export into the columns your system expects.
items.why: It contains identifiable student records. The task is mundane and the tool is capable, and neither of those facts changes where the data may go. Use an approved system.

items.text: Draft a job posting for an open advising position.
items.why: Public-facing, non-confidential, and heavily patterned. Read it before it posts — job postings carry legal weight and inherited boilerplate is where trouble hides.

items.text: Rewrite the withdrawal policy at an eighth-grade reading level for the website.
items.why: An excellent use, and one that genuinely helps students. Review closely: plain-language rewrites drop qualifiers, and in policy the qualifiers are frequently the point.

items.text: Check whether a 40-item event checklist has any blank fields.
items.why: A mechanical completeness check where you can verify the answer in seconds. Spot-check a few and move on.

It will write you a fluent one. It will also be generic in a way your supervisor recognises immediately, and you will have handed away the one document that is supposed to be your account of your own year.

items.text: Answer an email from a parent asking about their adult child's grades.
items.why: The trap is that this looks like routine correspondence. It is a FERPA question about what you may disclose and to whom, and the answer depends on facts a tool does not have.

items.text: Draft the agenda for next week's staff meeting from last month's action items.
items.why: Internal, low stakes, and errors are visible to everyone in the room within a minute. If an item is missing, somebody says so.

items.text: Write a memo recommending which of three vendors to select.
items.why: The recommendation is the work. It can help you organise the comparison once you have decided, but if it makes the decision you cannot defend it when procurement asks why.

steps.explain: The board packet and the roster are the two most people place too far to the right. Both are ordinary tasks a tool handles well — and both fail silently, one by dropping something nobody notices and the other by moving protected data somewhere it should not be.

steps.title: The rule underneath all twelve
steps.body: Look back at where the line fell.
steps.prompt: What actually separates the left of the line from the right?

options.text: Whether a mistake would be visible to me before it reached anyone else.
options.feedback: That is the rule. Drafting an email, reformatting notes, checking a list — you see the error while it is still yours. Summaries and reformatted records fail quietly, and by the time anyone notices, it is in somebody else's hands.
Difficulty barely correlates. The self-evaluation is easy and belongs to you; the plain-language rewrite is harder and delegates well.
The board packet summary is the fastest item on the list and the most dangerous. Time saved is what makes a bad delegation tempting, not what makes it safe.

options.text: Whether the tool is good at that kind of work.
options.feedback: It is good at all twelve. That is precisely why capability is useless as a decision rule — if you sort by what it can do, everything ends up on the right.
